findings.head: le:death-of-spouse:pause | HIGH | "Very few financial deadlines fall in the first weeks."
findings.text:
Why: if health coverage came through the spouse's job, the survivor faces real clocks (COBRA notice, a 60-day Marketplace window). The step says to "secure cash" but not how.
Fix: "One exception: if your health insurance came through your spouse's job, check COBRA, the Marketplace (60 days) or Medicaid now."

findings.head: le:death-of-spouse:pause or claims | HIGH | omission: the deceased's debts
findings.text:
Why: collectors often contact surviving spouses. In most states, outside community-property states, a survivor isn't personally liable for a spouse's individual debts unless they were joint or co-signed. Grieving survivors often pay anyway.
Fix: "You generally don't owe your spouse's individual debts unless you co-signed or live in a community-property state. Don't pay from your own money until you've checked. The estate handles them."

findings.head: le:death-of-spouse:notify | HIGH | "survivor benefits as early as age 60"
findings.text:
Why: a younger widow or widower caring for a child under 16 can get benefits at any age, and the children can get benefits too. A young parent reads "age 60" and assumes nothing is available. The one-time death payment isn't mentioned either.
Fix: "If you're caring for the deceased's child under 16, or if you are disabled, you may get benefits earlier. Children can also get benefits, and there is a one-time death payment."

findings.head: le:death-of-spouse:claims | MED | "the choice matters if the survivor is under 59½"
findings.text:
Why: it doesn't say which way it matters. A survivor under 59½ who treats the IRA as their own and then withdraws can owe the 10% they would have avoided by keeping it as an inherited IRA.
Fix: "If you're under 59½ and may need the money, keeping it as an inherited IRA lets you withdraw without the 10% additional tax; treating it as your own does not."

findings.head: le:death-of-spouse:taxes | LOW | "the widow's tax trap"
findings.text:
Why: the title is gendered and leans on jargon.
Fix: "Plan for the survivor's tax squeeze".

findings.head: le:death-of-spouse:pause — HIGH (overgeneralization)
findings.text:
Phrase: "Very few financial deadlines fall in the first weeks."
Why: True for selling assets, but it hides three clocks:
- If the household was on the deceased spouse's employer plan, COBRA (up to 36 months) and its notice rules start now.
- A qualified disclaimer must generally be made within 9 months and before accepting the asset.
- Portability of the deceased spouse's unused estate-tax exemption needs a Form 706, even when no tax is due. This is the item most often missed at this event, and the IRS's simplified relief window is up to 5 years.
Addition: "A few clocks start now: health coverage through the late spouse's employer (COBRA), the 9-month limit for disclaiming an inheritance, and the estate-tax return that preserves the unused exemption for you (portability), which is often worth filing even when no tax is owed."

findings.head: le:death-of-spouse:notify — MED (overgeneralization)
findings.text:
Phrase: "A surviving spouse can receive survivor benefits as early as age 60"
Why: The exception matters most for young widows and widowers. Benefits are available at any age when caring for the deceased's child under 16, and from 50 if disabled. Children under 18 get their own benefits.
Rewrite: "...as early as 60 (50 if disabled, and at any age while caring for the deceased's child under 16), and unmarried children under 18 can receive benefits of their own."

findings.head: le:death-of-spouse:taxes — MED (interaction with the pause step)
findings.text:
Missing:
- The surviving spouse keeps the full joint home-sale exclusion ({{fig:sec121_exclusion_mfj}}) only if the home is sold within two years of the death, so "selling the house can wait" has an expiry.
- Single-filer brackets also hit Medicare IRMAA tiers.
Addition: "A surviving spouse can still exclude up to the joint home-sale amount if the home is sold within two years of the death; single-filer status can also trigger Medicare surcharges, which can be appealed for a death in the family."

findings.head: le:death-of-spouse:claims — LOW
findings.text:
Missing: claiming or re-titling an asset can count as accepting it, which rules out disclaiming it (for example, to a bypass trust or to the children).
Addition: "Decide whether to disclaim any account before claiming or re-titling it."

le:death-of-spouse:pause.title: Make no irreversible decisions; secure cash for the next few months
le:death-of-spouse:pause.body: A few clocks start now, and the rest can wait. If your health coverage came through your spouse's employer, the COBRA and Marketplace windows begin when that coverage ends (60 days to act), and a decision to disclaim an inheritance must generally be made within 9 months and before you accept the asset. Selling the house, moving, or taking a lump sum can wait. Locate the will, policies and account statements, and get several certified copies of the death certificate — most institutions ask for one.
le:death-of-spouse:pause.plain: A few clocks start now, and the rest can wait. If your health insurance came through your spouse's job, the COBRA and Marketplace windows start when that coverage ends (you have 60 days to act), and if you want to turn down an inheritance you generally must do it within 9 months and before you accept it. Selling the house, moving, or taking a lump sum can wait. Find the will, insurance policies and account statements, and get several certified copies of the death certificate — most companies will ask for one.
props: A few deadlines start now; the rest can wait
Irreversible moves (sell house, move, lump sum) can wait
Get several certified death certificates; most institutions ask for one
COBRA and Marketplace windows start at loss of spouse-employer coverage; 60 days
A disclaimer must generally be made within 9 months and before accepting the asset

le:death-of-spouse:notify.title: Notify Social Security and claim survivor benefits
le:death-of-spouse:notify.body: Report the death to the Social Security Administration (funeral homes often do this). A surviving spouse can receive survivor benefits as early as age 60 (50 if disabled), and at any age while not remarried and caring for the deceased's child who is under 16 or disabled and entitled to child's benefits; the children themselves can receive benefits while under 18 (19 if still in secondary school), and there is a one-time lump-sum death payment. Switching between your own and the survivor benefit later can be worth comparing.
le:death-of-spouse:notify.plain: Tell the Social Security Administration about the death (the funeral home often does this). A surviving spouse can get survivor benefits as early as age 60 (50 if disabled), and at any age if they have not remarried and are caring for the deceased's child who is under 16 or disabled and qualifies for child's benefits. The children can get benefits of their own while under 18 (19 if still in high school), and there is a one-time lump-sum death payment. Later, you may be able to switch between the survivor benefit and your own; compare which pays more and when.
props: Report the death to SSA; funeral homes often do
Switching between own and survivor benefit later is worth comparing
Age 50 if disabled; any age while caring for the deceased's entitled child who is under 16 or disabled
Children receive benefits under 18 (19 if a secondary-school student)
There is a one-time lump-sum death payment
The any-age benefit requires that the surviving spouse has not remarried

le:death-of-spouse:claims.title: File life-insurance claims and re-title accounts
le:death-of-spouse:claims.body: Life insurance and retirement accounts pay to the named beneficiary directly. A surviving spouse who inherits an IRA can treat it as their own, roll it over, or keep it as an inherited IRA — the choice matters if the survivor is under 59½.
le:death-of-spouse:claims.plain: Life insurance and retirement accounts pay the named beneficiary directly. A surviving spouse who inherits an IRA can treat it as their own, roll it over, or keep it as an inherited IRA. The choice matters if the surviving spouse is under 59½.
props: Life insurance and retirement accounts pay the named beneficiary directly
A spouse can treat an inherited IRA as own, roll it over, or keep it inherited

le:death-of-spouse:taxes.title: Plan for the widow's tax trap
le:death-of-spouse:taxes.body: You can still file jointly for the year of death. After that, a survivor with a dependent child can file as a qualifying surviving spouse for two more years; otherwise the survivor files single — often with similar income but narrower brackets. Inherited assets generally receive a stepped-up basis, and in community-property states both halves of community property can.
le:death-of-spouse:taxes.plain: You can still file a joint return for the year your spouse died. After that, if you have a dependent child, you can file as a qualifying surviving spouse for two more years. Otherwise you file as single — often with about the same income but narrower tax brackets. Inherited assets usually get a stepped-up cost basis, and in community-property states both halves of shared property can.
props: Joint filing allowed for the year of death
QSS status for two more years with a dependent child
Otherwise single, often similar income with narrower brackets
Inherited assets generally get a stepped-up basis; community property both halves

le:death-of-spouse:update.title: Update your own estate documents and beneficiaries
le:death-of-spouse:update.body: Your will, powers of attorney and beneficiary forms probably name your spouse. Replace them, and re-run the diagnostic for a one-person household.
le:death-of-spouse:update.plain: Your own will, powers of attorney and beneficiary forms probably name your spouse. Replace them, and take the diagnostic again as a one-person household.
props: Own documents probably name the spouse
Re-run the diagnostic for one person
